novel_idea.topic_thesis: Autonomous permissions should expire with the doctrine that justified them; otherwise a well-aligned agent becomes a confident executor of stale strategy.
novel_idea.angle: Shift agent governance from one-time approval to version-bound autonomy: permissions must be reviewed when the underlying doctrine ages, changes, or meets contradictory evidence.
novel_idea.hook: The most dangerous permission in an AI system is the one that outlived its premise.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Organizations commonly evaluate an agent, confirm shared context, and then grant broader permissions. But doctrine has a half-life: its premises become stale as markets, obligations, and operating reality change. An agent can therefore remain technically capable and perfectly faithful while executing yesterday’s strategy against customers, money, production code, or other consequential systems. Permissions should be bound to a specific doctrine version and reconsidered when that doctrine expires or reality contradicts it. This is distinct from checking alignment before granting access; it governs what happens after a previously valid authorization becomes unsafe.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest prior post argues that humans and machines should pass the same Context Checksum before autonomous permissions expand. This argument addresses a different lifecycle failure and operator decision: permissions that were valid when granted but remain active after their governing doctrine has aged. The substantive delta is from initial alignment testing to ongoing authorization expiry tied to doctrine freshness.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source defines doctrine half-life as how long doctrine remains valid, current, and understood before drift or world change makes it stale. It states that agents require current doctrine, bounded permissions, evaluations, stop conditions, escalation triggers, and feedback paths; asks who is accountable when doctrine ages but an agent keeps acting; and warns that stale doctrine can regulate confidently from a false model. The Minimum Viable Coherence Program also ties permission levels to doctrine maturity and requires reality-driven doctrine updates.

An agent can be perfectly aligned and still do damage.

The failure is Doctrine Half-Life: the strategy changes, but the permission survives. A workflow approved once keeps acting from premises the organization no longer believes.

Imagine a pricing agent authorized to discount aggressively under a growth strategy. Margin pressure later changes the doctrine. If the agent retains its permission, it will execute yesterday’s strategy with today’s speed and confidence.

The dangerous agent is not always the rogue one. It is often the faithful executor of a dead map.

payload.body_text:
An agent can pass every evaluation and become unsafe the moment the doctrine changes.

Doctrine has a half-life: the period during which its premises remain valid, current, and understood. Autonomous authority should inherit that expiration.

Consider an agent approved to issue customer credits under version 12 of pricing doctrine. Version 13 changes margin limits and escalation rules. If the agent keeps its old permissions, it may execute perfectly against a map the organization has already abandoned.

Tie every autonomous permission to the doctrine version that authorized it. When that version expires, authority should narrow automatically until the agent is re-evaluated against the new map.
